     1	Nurse-Led Discharge Planning on Acute Medical Wards: A Stepped-Wedge Evaluation
     2	Evaluation report, September 2025. Department of Nursing Research and Practice Development,
     3	Calderbrook General Hospital.
     4	Abstract
     5	Background. Delays in discharging patients who are well enough to leave hospital lengthen
     6	hospital stays and reduce the number of beds available for new admissions. We evaluated a
     7	nurse-led discharge planning model on six acute medical wards.
     8	Methods. The model combined a dedicated discharge coordinator nurse on each ward, an
     9	expected date of discharge set within 24 hours of admission, daily board rounds and
    10	criteria-led discharge. Wards moved from usual care to the new model in a stepped-wedge
    11	sequence between April 2024 and March 2025. The primary outcome was length of stay.
    12	Results. The evaluation included 6,948 admissions. Mean length of stay fell from 7.9 to 7.1
    13	days, an adjusted reduction of 0.8 days. Emergency readmission within 30 days was slightly
    14	lower in the intervention period, and more patients left hospital before noon.
    15	Conclusions. Nurse-led discharge planning shortened hospital stays without an increase in
    16	readmissions or deaths. The model could be extended to other wards.
    17	
    18	1 Introduction
    19	Calderbrook General Hospital has operated at more than 95% bed occupancy for most of the
    20	past three years. On the acute medical wards, a large share of bed-days is used by patients
    21	who are medically fit to leave but are waiting for tests, medicines, transport or support at
    22	home. Discharges are often left until late in the day, which delays admissions from the
    23	emergency department.
    24	National guidance encourages hospitals to plan discharge from the point of admission, to set
    25	an expected date of discharge for every patient and to discharge patients earlier in the
    26	day. Earlier attempts at Calderbrook to introduce these practices relied on ward managers
    27	and medical teams and were not sustained.
    28	In 2023 the nursing directorate proposed a nurse-led model of discharge planning, in which a
    29	dedicated nurse would take responsibility for preparing each patient's discharge from the
    30	day of admission. This report presents the evaluation of that model on six acute medical
    31	wards over twelve months.
    32	2 Literature review
    33	Discharge planning has been studied extensively. A review of 30 randomised trials by Marlow
    34	and Ince (2018) found that structured discharge planning reduced mean length of stay by 0.7
    35	days and reduced readmissions at three months, although the effect on readmissions within 30
    36	days was uncertain. Okafor and colleagues (2020) reported that criteria-led discharge
    37	reduced mean length of stay by 0.5 days in a cluster trial in eight hospitals, with
    38	emergency readmission within 30 days of 12.8% in both arms.
    39	Other studies have focused on the timing of discharge. Lindqvist (2021) found that the share
    40	of patients discharged before noon rose from 15% to 24% after daily board rounds were
    41	introduced in a teaching hospital. The workload implications are less clear: Prescott (2019)
    42	estimated that nurse-led discharge required 31 minutes of additional registered nurse time
    43	per patient, while Haddad and Byrne (2022) found no change in overtime hours.
    44	Few studies have evaluated a combined model in a district general hospital, and fewer still
    45	have measured both patient outcomes and nursing time.
    46	
    47	3 Methods
    48	3.1 Setting and design
    49	The evaluation took place on six acute medical wards with a total of 168 beds. We used a
    50	stepped-wedge design: all wards began in the control period, and one ward moved to the
    51	intervention every two months, in an order chosen by lottery, until all six wards were using
    52	the new model.
    53	3.2 The intervention
    54	Each ward appointed a discharge coordinator, a band 6 registered nurse working on weekdays,
    55	funded at 1.0 whole-time equivalent per ward. The coordinator set an expected date of
    56	discharge within 24 hours of admission, led a daily board round at 09:00, arranged
    57	medicines, transport and community referrals, and authorised criteria-led discharge when
    58	agreed clinical criteria were met. Ward managers and coordinators received two half-day
    59	training sessions before each ward moved to the intervention.
    60	3.3 Outcomes
    61	The primary outcome was length of stay in days. Secondary outcomes were emergency
    62	readmission within 30 days, death within 30 days of discharge, the proportion of patients
    63	discharged before noon, and bed-days lost to delayed discharge. Patients completed a
    64	readiness for discharge questionnaire, scored from 0 to 10, on the day of discharge.
    65	Nursing time was measured by work sampling on two randomly chosen days each month. Ward
    66	staff nurses were invited to complete an anonymous workload survey in March 2025.
    67	3.4 Analysis
    68	Outcomes were compared between control and intervention periods using mixed-effects models
    69	with a random effect for ward and a fixed effect for calendar month, to allow for seasonal
    70	trends. Results are reported with 95% confidence intervals (CI), and a significance level of
    71	0.05 was specified in advance.
    72	3.5 Data sources
    73	Admission, discharge and readmission data were taken from the hospital's patient
    74	administration system. Deaths after discharge were identified through the national death
    75	register, and delayed discharges were taken from the daily ward status return.
    76	3.6 Patient and public involvement
    77	
    78	Two former patients and a carer sat on the evaluation steering group. They helped to word
    79	the readiness for discharge questionnaire and advised on how to approach patients on the day
    80	of discharge.
    81	
    82	4 Results
    83	4.1 Participants
    84	The evaluation included 6,948 admissions of adults aged 18 and over: 3,302 during control
    85	periods and 3,646 during intervention periods. Patient characteristics were similar in the
    86	two periods (Table 1).
    87	Table 1. Characteristics of admissions by study period
    88	Characteristic Control period Intervention period
    89	Admissions 3,302 3,646
    90	Mean age, years 74.1 73.8
    91	Women, % 52 51
    92	Admitted through the emergency department, % 88 89
    93	Living alone, % 34 33
    94	Aged 80 and over, % 32 32
    95	4.2 Length of stay
    96	Mean length of stay was 7.9 days in the control period and 7.1 days in the intervention
    97	period. After adjustment for ward and calendar month, the new model reduced mean length of
    98	stay by 0.8 days (95% CI 0.5 to 1.1). Table 2 summarises the primary and secondary outcomes.
    99	Table 2. Primary and secondary outcomes by study period
   100	Outcome Control period Intervention period Adjusted effect (95% CI)
   101	Mean length of stay, days 7.9 7.1 -0.8 days (-1.1 to -0.5)
   102	Emergency readmission within 30 days, % 15.1 14.2 OR 0.93 (0.79 to 1.09)
   103	Discharged before noon, % 18.6 29.3 OR 1.84 (1.58 to 2.14)
   104	Death within 30 days of discharge, % 5.4 5.2 OR 0.97 (0.80 to 1.18)
   105	Readiness for discharge score, 0 to 10 6.8 7.4 +0.6 (0.3 to 0.9)
   106	
   107	4.3 Readmissions and mortality
   108	Emergency readmission within 30 days occurred after 14.2% of discharges in the intervention
   109	period and 15.1% of discharges in the control period (adjusted odds ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.79
   110	to 1.09). However, the difference was not statistically significant. Mortality within 30
   111	days of discharge was similar in the two periods (Table 2). The most common reasons for
   112	readmission in both periods were respiratory infection, heart failure and urinary infection.
   113	4.4 Discharge timing and delays
   114	The proportion of patients leaving hospital before noon rose under the new model (Table 2).
   115	Bed-days lost to delayed discharge, counted from the day a patient was recorded as medically
   116	fit to leave, fell from 1,184 in the control period to 902 in the intervention period. This
   117	fall was driven mainly by quicker arrangement of medicines to take home and of transport.
   118	4.5 Readiness for discharge
   119	Patients discharged under the new model reported feeling better prepared to leave hospital.
   120	The mean readiness for discharge score rose from 6.8 to 7.4 out of 10. Questionnaires were
   121	returned by 61% of patients, and the return rate was lower among patients aged 80 and over.
   122	
   123	4.6 Results by age group
   124	The effect of the new model differed by age (Table 3). Among patients aged 80 years and
   125	over, mean length of stay fell by 1.4 days, from 10.4 to 9.0 days. This effect was almost
   126	three times the reduction seen in patients under 80, whose length of stay fell by 0.5 days.
   127	The subgroup analysis was exploratory and had not been specified in the study protocol.
   128	Table 3. Mean length of stay in days by age group and study period
   129	Age group Control period Intervention period Difference
   130	18 to 64 5.6 5.3 -0.3
   131	65 to 79 7.6 6.9 -0.7
   132	80 and over 10.4 9.0 -1.4
   133	All ages 7.9 7.1 -0.8
   134	Patients aged 80 and over made up 32% of admissions but accounted for 42% of bed-days in the
   135	control period. Most of the additional reduction in this group came from fewer days spent
   136	waiting for care packages at home.
   137	
   138	4.7 Nursing time and workload
   139	Work sampling showed that discharge coordinators spent a mean of 26 minutes on each
   140	discharge, covering board rounds, referrals, medicines and contact with families. Time spent
   141	by ward staff nurses on discharge paperwork fell from 52 to 34 minutes per shift.
   142	In the staff survey, 64% of ward nurses said that their workload was about the same as or
   143	lighter than before the new model, and 22% said it was heavier. Only 41% of ward nurses
   144	returned the survey, so these views may not be representative of all ward staff.
   145	4.8 Implementation
   146	An expected date of discharge was recorded within 24 hours for 87% of admissions in the
   147	intervention period, and board rounds took place on 94% of weekdays. Criteria-led discharge
   148	was used for 19% of discharges, most often at weekends when no senior doctor was on the
   149	ward.
   150	5 Discussion
   151	The nurse-led model shortened hospital stays by a margin similar to that reported in earlier
   152	trials, and the largest gains were among patients aged 80 and over, who occupy the most
   153	bed-days. These gains came without an increase in readmissions or deaths.
   154	The reduction of 0.8 days is close to the 0.7 days reported in the review by Marlow and Ince
   155	(2018), and larger than the 0.5 days found for criteria-led discharge alone by Okafor and
   156	colleagues (2020). The rise in discharges before noon was larger than in earlier reports,
   157	which suggests that the daily board round was an important part of the model.
   158	The workload findings need careful interpretation. The time saved by ward staff nurses was
   159	largely offset by the time spent by the coordinators, so the model redistributed discharge
   160	work to a dedicated role rather than reducing total nursing time.
   161	
   162	6 Limitations
   163	This was a single-site evaluation, and ward staff could not be blinded to the intervention.
   164	Although the stepped-wedge design and adjustment for calendar month reduce the influence of
   165	seasonal trends, other changes during the year, such as new community care contracts, may
   166	have contributed to shorter stays. We did not undertake an economic evaluation, so the costs
   167	of the coordinator posts have not been compared with the value of the bed-days saved.
   168	7 Conclusions
   169	Nurse-led discharge planning reduced length of stay on acute medical wards without
   170	increasing readmissions. The hospital should consider extending the model to the remaining
   171	medical wards, with continued monitoring of readmissions and staff workload.
   172	Acknowledgements
   173	We thank the ward managers, discharge coordinators and patients who took part, and the
   174	hospital's information team for extracting admission data.
   175	Ethics and data availability
   176	The evaluation was registered as a service evaluation with the hospital's clinical audit
   177	department, and research ethics committee review was not required. Patients could decline
   178	the readiness questionnaire without any effect on their care. Aggregate data are available
   179	from the Department of Nursing Research on request.
   180	Funding and conflicts of interest
   181	The evaluation was funded by the Calderbrook Hospital Charity. The authors are employed by
   182	the hospital, and two of the authors helped to design the nurse-led model.
   183	References
   184	Haddad N, Byrne S (2022). Overtime and discharge planning on medical wards. Nursing
   185	Workforce Journal 12: 88-97.
   186	Lindqvist E (2021). Board rounds and the timing of hospital discharge. Hospital Flow
   187	Quarterly 5: 31-40.
   188	Marlow T, Ince G (2018). Structured discharge planning: a review of 30 randomised trials.
   189	Review of Hospital Care 22: 140-161.
   190	Okafor U, Brennan J, Silva M (2020). Criteria-led discharge in eight hospitals: a cluster
   191	
   192	trial. Acute Medicine Research 14: 201-213.
   193	Prescott D (2019). Measuring the nursing time cost of discharge. Journal of Ward Practice 9:
   194	57-66.

     5	Purpose
     6	
     7	This paper summarises the evaluation of the nurse-led discharge planning model that ran on six acute medical wards between April 2024 and March 2025, and asks the Board to approve extending the model.
     8	
     9	Background
    10	
    11	The acute medical wards have run at more than 95% bed occupancy for most of the last three years, and delays in discharge are a major cause of long waits for beds in the emergency department. The nurse-led model was designed to plan each discharge from the day of admission, with a dedicated coordinator nurse on every ward.
    12	
    13	Key findings
    14	
    15	The evaluation covered 6,948 admissions. Under the new model, the average hospital stay was 1.2 days shorter, which is equivalent to freeing several beds every day across the six wards.
    16	
    17	Readmissions within 30 days fell from 15.1% to 14.2%, and patients reported feeling better prepared to go home. Patients aged 80 and over benefited most.
    18	
    19	Ward nurses now spend less time on discharge paperwork, and most nurses who responded to the staff survey said their workload was the same or lighter.
    20	
    21	Resources
    22	
    23	The model requires one discharge coordinator nurse per ward. The six coordinator posts are funded from the hospital charity grant until March 2026. No savings have yet been calculated, and Finance will develop the economic case for the Board in early 2026.
    24	
    25	Recommendation
    26	
    27	The Board is asked to approve extending nurse-led discharge planning to the four remaining medical wards from April 2026, subject to the economic case.
    28	
    29	Risks
    30	
    31	The main risks are recruiting experienced band 6 nurses to the coordinator posts and keeping daily board rounds going during periods of high demand.
    32	
    33	Next steps
    34	
    35	If the Board approves the extension, recruitment to the four new coordinator posts will begin in January 2026, and the Chief Nurse will report progress to the Quality Committee every quarter.

     2	Evaluation report, September 2025. Department of Nursing Research and Practice Development,
     3	Calderbrook General Hospital.
     4	Abstract
     5	Background. Delays in discharging patients who are well enough to leave hospital lengthen
     6	hospital stays and reduce the number of beds available for new admissions. We evaluated a
     7	nurse-led discharge planning model on six acute medical wards.
     8	Methods. The model combined a dedicated discharge coordinator nurse on each ward, an
     9	expected date of discharge set within 24 hours of admission, daily board rounds and
    10	criteria-led discharge. Wards moved from usual care to the new model in a stepped-wedge
    11	sequence between April 2024 and March 2025. The primary outcome was length of stay.
    12	Results. The evaluation included 6,948 admissions. Mean length of stay fell from 7.9 to 7.1
    13	days, an adjusted reduction of 0.8 days. Emergency readmission within 30 days was slightly
    14	lower in the intervention period, and more patients left hospital before noon.
    15	Conclusions. Nurse-led discharge planning shortened hospital stays without an increase in
    16	readmissions or deaths. The model could be extended to other wards.
    17	
    18	1 Introduction
    19	Calderbrook General Hospital has operated at more than 95% bed occupancy for most of the
    20	past three years. On the acute medical wards, a large share of bed-days is used by patients
    21	who are medically fit to leave but are waiting for tests, medicines, transport or support at
    22	home. Discharges are often left until late in the day, which delays admissions from the
    23	emergency department.
    24	National guidance encourages hospitals to plan discharge from the point of admission, to set
    25	an expected date of discharge for every patient and to discharge patients earlier in the
    26	day. Earlier attempts at Calderbrook to introduce these practices relied on ward managers
    27	and medical teams and were not sustained.
    28	In 2023 the nursing directorate proposed a nurse-led model of discharge planning, in which a
    29	dedicated nurse would take responsibility for preparing each patient's discharge from the
    30	day of admission. This report presents the evaluation of that model on six acute medical
    31	wards over twelve months.
    32	2 Literature review
    33	Discharge planning has been studied extensively. A review of 30 randomised trials by Marlow
    34	and Ince (2018) found that structured discharge planning reduced mean length of stay by 0.7
    35	days and reduced readmissions at three months, although the effect on readmissions within 30
    36	days was uncertain. Okafor and colleagues (2020) reported that criteria-led discharge
    37	reduced mean length of stay by 0.5 days in a cluster trial in eight hospitals, with
    38	emergency readmission within 30 days of 12.8% in both arms.
    39	Other studies have focused on the timing of discharge. Lindqvist (2021) found that the share
    40	of patients discharged before noon rose from 15% to 24% after daily board rounds were
    41	introduced in a teaching hospital. The workload implications are less clear: Prescott (2019)
    42	estimated that nurse-led discharge required 31 minutes of additional registered nurse time
    43	per patient, while Haddad and Byrne (2022) found no change in overtime hours.
    44	Few studies have evaluated a combined model in a district general hospital, and fewer still
    45	have measured both patient outcomes and nursing time.
    46	
    47	3 Methods
    48	3.1 Setting and design
    49	The evaluation took place on six acute medical wards with a total of 168 beds. We used a
    50	stepped-wedge design: all wards began in the control period, and one ward moved to the
    51	intervention every two months, in an order chosen by lottery, until all six wards were using
    52	the new model.
    53	3.2 The intervention
    54	Each ward appointed a discharge coordinator, a band 6 registered nurse working on weekdays,
    55	funded at 1.0 whole-time equivalent per ward. The coordinator set an expected date of
    56	discharge within 24 hours of admission, led a daily board round at 09:00, arranged
    57	medicines, transport and community referrals, and authorised criteria-led discharge when
    58	agreed clinical criteria were met. Ward managers and coordinators received two half-day
    59	training sessions before each ward moved to the intervention.
    60	3.3 Outcomes
    61	The primary outcome was length of stay in days. Secondary outcomes were emergency
    62	readmission within 30 days, death within 30 days of discharge, the proportion of patients
    63	discharged before noon, and bed-days lost to delayed discharge. Patients completed a
    64	readiness for discharge questionnaire, scored from 0 to 10, on the day of discharge.
    65	Nursing time was measured by work sampling on two randomly chosen days each month. Ward
    66	staff nurses were invited to complete an anonymous workload survey in March 2025.
    67	3.4 Analysis
    68	Outcomes were compared between control and intervention periods using mixed-effects models
    69	with a random effect for ward and a fixed effect for calendar month, to allow for seasonal
    70	trends. Results are reported with 95% confidence intervals (CI), and a significance level of
    71	0.05 was specified in advance.
    72	3.5 Data sources
    73	Admission, discharge and readmission data were taken from the hospital's patient
    74	administration system. Deaths after discharge were identified through the national death
    75	register, and delayed discharges were taken from the daily ward status return.
    76	3.6 Patient and public involvement
    77	
    78	Two former patients and a carer sat on the evaluation steering group. They helped to word
    79	the readiness for discharge questionnaire and advised on how to approach patients on the day
    80	of discharge.
    81	
    82	4 Results
    83	4.1 Participants
    84	The evaluation included 6,948 admissions of adults aged 18 and over: 3,302 during control
    85	periods and 3,646 during intervention periods. Patient characteristics were similar in the
    86	two periods (Table 1).
    87	Table 1. Characteristics of admissions by study period
    88	Characteristic Control period Intervention period
    89	Admissions 3,302 3,646
    90	Mean age, years 74.1 73.8
    91	Women, % 52 51
    92	Admitted through the emergency department, % 88 89
    93	Living alone, % 34 33
    94	Aged 80 and over, % 32 32
    95	4.2 Length of stay
    96	Mean length of stay was 7.9 days in the control period and 7.1 days in the intervention
    97	period. After adjustment for ward and calendar month, the new model reduced mean length of
    98	stay by 0.8 days (95% CI 0.5 to 1.1). Table 2 summarises the primary and secondary outcomes.
    99	Table 2. Primary and secondary outcomes by study period
   100	Outcome Control period Intervention period Adjusted effect (95% CI)
   101	Mean length of stay, days 7.9 7.1 -0.8 days (-1.1 to -0.5)
   102	Emergency readmission within 30 days, % 15.1 14.2 OR 0.93 (0.79 to 1.09)
   103	Discharged before noon, % 18.6 29.3 OR 1.84 (1.58 to 2.14)
   104	Death within 30 days of discharge, % 5.4 5.2 OR 0.97 (0.80 to 1.18)
   105	Readiness for discharge score, 0 to 10 6.8 7.4 +0.6 (0.3 to 0.9)
   106	
   107	4.3 Readmissions and mortality
   108	Emergency readmission within 30 days occurred after 14.2% of discharges in the intervention
   109	period and 15.1% of discharges in the control period (adjusted odds ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.79
   110	to 1.09). However, the difference was not statistically significant. Mortality within 30
   111	days of discharge was similar in the two periods (Table 2). The most common reasons for
   112	readmission in both periods were respiratory infection, heart failure and urinary infection.
   113	4.4 Discharge timing and delays
   114	The proportion of patients leaving hospital before noon rose under the new model (Table 2).
   115	Bed-days lost to delayed discharge, counted from the day a patient was recorded as medically
   116	fit to leave, fell from 1,184 in the control period to 902 in the intervention period. This
   117	fall was driven mainly by quicker arrangement of medicines to take home and of transport.
   118	4.5 Readiness for discharge
   119	Patients discharged under the new model reported feeling better prepared to leave hospital.
   120	The mean readiness for discharge score rose from 6.8 to 7.4 out of 10. Questionnaires were
   121	returned by 61% of patients, and the return rate was lower among patients aged 80 and over.
   122	
   123	4.6 Results by age group
   124	The effect of the new model differed by age (Table 3). Among patients aged 80 years and
   125	over, mean length of stay fell by 1.4 days, from 10.4 to 9.0 days. This effect was almost
   126	three times the reduction seen in patients under 80, whose length of stay fell by 0.5 days.
   127	The subgroup analysis was exploratory and had not been specified in the study protocol.
   128	Table 3. Mean length of stay in days by age group and study period
   129	Age group Control period Intervention period Difference
   130	18 to 64 5.6 5.3 -0.3
   131	65 to 79 7.6 6.9 -0.7
   132	80 and over 10.4 9.0 -1.4
   133	All ages 7.9 7.1 -0.8
   134	Patients aged 80 and over made up 32% of admissions but accounted for 42% of bed-days in the
   135	control period. Most of the additional reduction in this group came from fewer days spent
   136	waiting for care packages at home.
   137	
   138	4.7 Nursing time and workload
   139	Work sampling showed that discharge coordinators spent a mean of 26 minutes on each
   140	discharge, covering board rounds, referrals, medicines and contact with families. Time spent
   141	by ward staff nurses on discharge paperwork fell from 52 to 34 minutes per shift.
   142	In the staff survey, 64% of ward nurses said that their workload was about the same as or
   143	lighter than before the new model, and 22% said it was heavier. Only 41% of ward nurses
   144	returned the survey, so these views may not be representative of all ward staff.
   145	4.8 Implementation
   146	An expected date of discharge was recorded within 24 hours for 87% of admissions in the
   147	intervention period, and board rounds took place on 94% of weekdays. Criteria-led discharge
   148	was used for 19% of discharges, most often at weekends when no senior doctor was on the
   149	ward.
   150	5 Discussion
   151	The nurse-led model shortened hospital stays by a margin similar to that reported in earlier
   152	trials, and the largest gains were among patients aged 80 and over, who occupy the most
   153	bed-days. These gains came without an increase in readmissions or deaths.
   154	The reduction of 0.8 days is close to the 0.7 days reported in the review by Marlow and Ince
   155	(2018), and larger than the 0.5 days found for criteria-led discharge alone by Okafor and
   156	colleagues (2020). The rise in discharges before noon was larger than in earlier reports,
   157	which suggests that the daily board round was an important part of the model.
   158	The workload findings need careful interpretation. The time saved by ward staff nurses was
   159	largely offset by the time spent by the coordinators, so the model redistributed discharge
   160	work to a dedicated role rather than reducing total nursing time.
   161	
   162	6 Limitations
   163	This was a single-site evaluation, and ward staff could not be blinded to the intervention.
   164	Although the stepped-wedge design and adjustment for calendar month reduce the influence of
   165	seasonal trends, other changes during the year, such as new community care contracts, may
   166	have contributed to shorter stays. We did not undertake an economic evaluation, so the costs
   167	of the coordinator posts have not been compared with the value of the bed-days saved.
   168	7 Conclusions
   169	Nurse-led discharge planning reduced length of stay on acute medical wards without
   170	increasing readmissions. The hospital should consider extending the model to the remaining
   171	medical wards, with continued monitoring of readmissions and staff workload.
   172	Acknowledgements
   173	We thank the ward managers, discharge coordinators and patients who took part, and the
   174	hospital's information team for extracting admission data.
   175	Ethics and data availability
   176	The evaluation was registered as a service evaluation with the hospital's clinical audit
   177	department, and research ethics committee review was not required. Patients could decline
   178	the readiness questionnaire without any effect on their care. Aggregate data are available
   179	from the Department of Nursing Research on request.
   180	Funding and conflicts of interest
   181	The evaluation was funded by the Calderbrook Hospital Charity. The authors are employed by
   182	the hospital, and two of the authors helped to design the nurse-led model.
   183	References
   184	Haddad N, Byrne S (2022). Overtime and discharge planning on medical wards. Nursing
   185	Workforce Journal 12: 88-97.
   186	Lindqvist E (2021). Board rounds and the timing of hospital discharge. Hospital Flow
   187	Quarterly 5: 31-40.
   188	Marlow T, Ince G (2018). Structured discharge planning: a review of 30 randomised trials.
   189	Review of Hospital Care 22: 140-161.
   190	Okafor U, Brennan J, Silva M (2020). Criteria-led discharge in eight hospitals: a cluster
   191	
   192	trial. Acute Medicine Research 14: 201-213.
   193	Prescott D (2019). Measuring the nursing time cost of discharge. Journal of Ward Practice 9:
   194	57-66.

     1	Nurse-Led Discharge Planning on Acute Medical Wards: A Stepped-Wedge Evaluation
     2	Evaluation report, September 2025. Department of Nursing Research and Practice Development,
     3	Calderbrook General Hospital.
     4	Abstract
     5	Background. Delays in discharging patients who are well enough to leave hospital lengthen
     6	hospital stays and reduce the number of beds available for new admissions. We evaluated a
     7	nurse-led discharge planning model on six acute medical wards.
     8	Methods. The model combined a dedicated discharge coordinator nurse on each ward, an
     9	expected date of discharge set within 24 hours of admission, daily board rounds and
    10	criteria-led discharge. Wards moved from usual care to the new model in a stepped-wedge
    11	sequence between April 2024 and March 2025. The primary outcome was length of stay.
    12	Results. The evaluation included 6,948 admissions. Mean length of stay fell from 7.9 to 7.1
    13	days, an adjusted reduction of 0.8 days. Emergency readmission within 30 days was slightly
    14	lower in the intervention period, and more patients left hospital before noon.
    15	Conclusions. Nurse-led discharge planning shortened hospital stays without an increase in
    16	readmissions or deaths. The model could be extended to other wards.
    17	
    18	1 Introduction
    19	Calderbrook General Hospital has operated at more than 95% bed occupancy for most of the
    20	past three years. On the acute medical wards, a large share of bed-days is used by patients
    21	who are medically fit to leave but are waiting for tests, medicines, transport or support at
    22	home. Discharges are often left until late in the day, which delays admissions from the
    23	emergency department.
    24	National guidance encourages hospitals to plan discharge from the point of admission, to set
    25	an expected date of discharge for every patient and to discharge patients earlier in the
    26	day. Earlier attempts at Calderbrook to introduce these practices relied on ward managers
    27	and medical teams and were not sustained.
    28	In 2023 the nursing directorate proposed a nurse-led model of discharge planning, in which a
    29	dedicated nurse would take responsibility for preparing each patient's discharge from the
    30	day of admission. This report presents the evaluation of that model on six acute medical
    31	wards over twelve months.
    32	2 Literature review
    33	Discharge planning has been studied extensively. A review of 30 randomised trials by Marlow
    34	and Ince (2018) found that structured discharge planning reduced mean length of stay by 0.7
    35	days and reduced readmissions at three months, although the effect on readmissions within 30
    36	days was uncertain. Okafor and colleagues (2020) reported that criteria-led discharge
    37	reduced mean length of stay by 0.5 days in a cluster trial in eight hospitals, with
    38	emergency readmission within 30 days of 12.8% in both arms.
    39	Other studies have focused on the timing of discharge. Lindqvist (2021) found that the share
    40	of patients discharged before noon rose from 15% to 24% after daily board rounds were
    41	introduced in a teaching hospital. The workload implications are less clear: Prescott (2019)
    42	estimated that nurse-led discharge required 31 minutes of additional registered nurse time
    43	per patient, while Haddad and Byrne (2022) found no change in overtime hours.
    44	Few studies have evaluated a combined model in a district general hospital, and fewer still
    45	have measured both patient outcomes and nursing time.
    46	
    47	3 Methods
    48	3.1 Setting and design
    49	The evaluation took place on six acute medical wards with a total of 168 beds. We used a
    50	stepped-wedge design: all wards began in the control period, and one ward moved to the
    51	intervention every two months, in an order chosen by lottery, until all six wards were using
    52	the new model.
    53	3.2 The intervention
    54	Each ward appointed a discharge coordinator, a band 6 registered nurse working on weekdays,
    55	funded at 1.0 whole-time equivalent per ward. The coordinator set an expected date of
    56	discharge within 24 hours of admission, led a daily board round at 09:00, arranged
    57	medicines, transport and community referrals, and authorised criteria-led discharge when
    58	agreed clinical criteria were met. Ward managers and coordinators received two half-day
    59	training sessions before each ward moved to the intervention.
    60	3.3 Outcomes
    61	The primary outcome was length of stay in days. Secondary outcomes were emergency
    62	readmission within 30 days, death within 30 days of discharge, the proportion of patients
    63	discharged before noon, and bed-days lost to delayed discharge. Patients completed a
    64	readiness for discharge questionnaire, scored from 0 to 10, on the day of discharge.
    65	Nursing time was measured by work sampling on two randomly chosen days each month. Ward
    66	staff nurses were invited to complete an anonymous workload survey in March 2025.
    67	3.4 Analysis
    68	Outcomes were compared between control and intervention periods using mixed-effects models
    69	with a random effect for ward and a fixed effect for calendar month, to allow for seasonal
    70	trends. Results are reported with 95% confidence intervals (CI), and a significance level of
    71	0.05 was specified in advance.
    72	3.5 Data sources
    73	Admission, discharge and readmission data were taken from the hospital's patient
    74	administration system. Deaths after discharge were identified through the national death
    75	register, and delayed discharges were taken from the daily ward status return.
    76	3.6 Patient and public involvement
    77	
    78	Two former patients and a carer sat on the evaluation steering group. They helped to word
    79	the readiness for discharge questionnaire and advised on how to approach patients on the day
    80	of discharge.
    81	
    82	4 Results
    83	4.1 Participants
    84	The evaluation included 6,948 admissions of adults aged 18 and over: 3,302 during control
    85	periods and 3,646 during intervention periods. Patient characteristics were similar in the
    86	two periods (Table 1).
    87	Table 1. Characteristics of admissions by study period
    88	Characteristic Control period Intervention period
    89	Admissions 3,302 3,646
    90	Mean age, years 74.1 73.8
    91	Women, % 52 51
    92	Admitted through the emergency department, % 88 89
    93	Living alone, % 34 33
    94	Aged 80 and over, % 32 32
    95	4.2 Length of stay
    96	Mean length of stay was 7.9 days in the control period and 7.1 days in the intervention
    97	period. After adjustment for ward and calendar month, the new model reduced mean length of
    98	stay by 0.8 days (95% CI 0.5 to 1.1). Table 2 summarises the primary and secondary outcomes.
    99	Table 2. Primary and secondary outcomes by study period
   100	Outcome Control period Intervention period Adjusted effect (95% CI)
   101	Mean length of stay, days 7.9 7.1 -0.8 days (-1.1 to -0.5)
   102	Emergency readmission within 30 days, % 15.1 14.2 OR 0.93 (0.79 to 1.09)
   103	Discharged before noon, % 18.6 29.3 OR 1.84 (1.58 to 2.14)
   104	Death within 30 days of discharge, % 5.4 5.2 OR 0.97 (0.80 to 1.18)
   105	Readiness for discharge score, 0 to 10 6.8 7.4 +0.6 (0.3 to 0.9)
   106	
   107	4.3 Readmissions and mortality
   108	Emergency readmission within 30 days occurred after 14.2% of discharges in the intervention
   109	period and 15.1% of discharges in the control period (adjusted odds ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.79
   110	to 1.09). However, the difference was not statistically significant. Mortality within 30
   111	days of discharge was similar in the two periods (Table 2). The most common reasons for
   112	readmission in both periods were respiratory infection, heart failure and urinary infection.
   113	4.4 Discharge timing and delays
   114	The proportion of patients leaving hospital before noon rose under the new model (Table 2).
   115	Bed-days lost to delayed discharge, counted from the day a patient was recorded as medically
   116	fit to leave, fell from 1,184 in the control period to 902 in the intervention period. This
   117	fall was driven mainly by quicker arrangement of medicines to take home and of transport.
   118	4.5 Readiness for discharge
   119	Patients discharged under the new model reported feeling better prepared to leave hospital.
   120	The mean readiness for discharge score rose from 6.8 to 7.4 out of 10. Questionnaires were
   121	returned by 61% of patients, and the return rate was lower among patients aged 80 and over.
   122	
   123	4.6 Results by age group
   124	The effect of the new model differed by age (Table 3). Among patients aged 80 years and
   125	over, mean length of stay fell by 1.4 days, from 10.4 to 9.0 days. This effect was almost
   126	three times the reduction seen in patients under 80, whose length of stay fell by 0.5 days.
   127	The subgroup analysis was exploratory and had not been specified in the study protocol.
   128	Table 3. Mean length of stay in days by age group and study period
   129	Age group Control period Intervention period Difference
   130	18 to 64 5.6 5.3 -0.3
   131	65 to 79 7.6 6.9 -0.7
   132	80 and over 10.4 9.0 -1.4
   133	All ages 7.9 7.1 -0.8
   134	Patients aged 80 and over made up 32% of admissions but accounted for 42% of bed-days in the
   135	control period. Most of the additional reduction in this group came from fewer days spent
   136	waiting for care packages at home.
   137	
   138	4.7 Nursing time and workload
   139	Work sampling showed that discharge coordinators spent a mean of 26 minutes on each
   140	discharge, covering board rounds, referrals, medicines and contact with families. Time spent
   141	by ward staff nurses on discharge paperwork fell from 52 to 34 minutes per shift.
   142	In the staff survey, 64% of ward nurses said that their workload was about the same as or
   143	lighter than before the new model, and 22% said it was heavier. Only 41% of ward nurses
   144	returned the survey, so these views may not be representative of all ward staff.
   145	4.8 Implementation
   146	An expected date of discharge was recorded within 24 hours for 87% of admissions in the
   147	intervention period, and board rounds took place on 94% of weekdays. Criteria-led discharge
   148	was used for 19% of discharges, most often at weekends when no senior doctor was on the
   149	ward.
   150	5 Discussion
   151	The nurse-led model shortened hospital stays by a margin similar to that reported in earlier
   152	trials, and the largest gains were among patients aged 80 and over, who occupy the most
   153	bed-days. These gains came without an increase in readmissions or deaths.
   154	The reduction of 0.8 days is close to the 0.7 days reported in the review by Marlow and Ince
   155	(2018), and larger than the 0.5 days found for criteria-led discharge alone by Okafor and
   156	colleagues (2020). The rise in discharges before noon was larger than in earlier reports,
   157	which suggests that the daily board round was an important part of the model.
   158	The workload findings need careful interpretation. The time saved by ward staff nurses was
   159	largely offset by the time spent by the coordinators, so the model redistributed discharge
   160	work to a dedicated role rather than reducing total nursing time.
   161	
   162	6 Limitations
   163	This was a single-site evaluation, and ward staff could not be blinded to the intervention.
   164	Although the stepped-wedge design and adjustment for calendar month reduce the influence of
   165	seasonal trends, other changes during the year, such as new community care contracts, may
   166	have contributed to shorter stays. We did not undertake an economic evaluation, so the costs
   167	of the coordinator posts have not been compared with the value of the bed-days saved.
   168	7 Conclusions
   169	Nurse-led discharge planning reduced length of stay on acute medical wards without
   170	increasing readmissions. The hospital should consider extending the model to the remaining
   171	medical wards, with continued monitoring of readmissions and staff workload.
   172	Acknowledgements
   173	We thank the ward managers, discharge coordinators and patients who took part, and the
   174	hospital's information team for extracting admission data.
   175	Ethics and data availability
   176	The evaluation was registered as a service evaluation with the hospital's clinical audit
   177	department, and research ethics committee review was not required. Patients could decline
   178	the readiness questionnaire without any effect on their care. Aggregate data are available
   179	from the Department of Nursing Research on request.
   180	Funding and conflicts of interest
   181	The evaluation was funded by the Calderbrook Hospital Charity. The authors are employed by
   182	the hospital, and two of the authors helped to design the nurse-led model.
   183	References
   184	Haddad N, Byrne S (2022). Overtime and discharge planning on medical wards. Nursing
   185	Workforce Journal 12: 88-97.
   186	Lindqvist E (2021). Board rounds and the timing of hospital discharge. Hospital Flow
   187	Quarterly 5: 31-40.
   188	Marlow T, Ince G (2018). Structured discharge planning: a review of 30 randomised trials.
   189	Review of Hospital Care 22: 140-161.
   190	Okafor U, Brennan J, Silva M (2020). Criteria-led discharge in eight hospitals: a cluster
   191	
   192	trial. Acute Medicine Research 14: 201-213.
   193	Prescott D (2019). Measuring the nursing time cost of discharge. Journal of Ward Practice 9:
   194	57-66.

     1	Borrowing instead of buying: evaluation of the Brackenford Library of Things pilot, April 2023 to March 2025
     2	Northfold Social Research, for Brackenford Libraries. Final report, September 2025.
     3	Abstract
     4	The Brackenford Library of Things lends household tools and equipment from three branch
     5	libraries for a small fee. This report evaluates the first two years of the pilot, from
     6	April 2023 to March 2025, using membership and loan records, a survey of borrowers and the
     7	checks that staff make when items are returned. Almost 2,000 residents registered as
     8	borrowers, and loans grew by 64 percent between the first and second years. Borrowers
     9	reported modest savings, and most items came back in good condition. Registrations from
    10	deprived neighbourhoods were roughly in line with their share of the town's population. We
    11	recommend that the scheme continues, with changes to how damage is recorded and how new
    12	items are chosen.
    13	1 Introduction
    14	Libraries of things apply the familiar library model to objects that households need only
    15	occasionally, such as drills, gazebos and sewing machines. Their supporters argue that
    16	borrowing saves money, reduces the number of rarely used items that people buy, and brings
    17	people into libraries who would not otherwise visit.
    18	Brackenford Libraries opened its Library of Things in April 2023 with a grant of GBP 96,000
    19	from the Halden Foundation, which also funded this evaluation. The pilot ran from three of
    20	the town's seven branch libraries: Central, Eastgate and Millbrook.
    21	
    22	Items could be reserved online and collected from any of the three branches, and loans
    23	lasted up to seven days. This report sets out what the pilot achieved against the aims
    24	agreed with the funder: to reach a broad range of residents, to build regular use, to save
    25	households money and to reduce waste. Section 2 summarises earlier evaluations of similar
    26	schemes, Section 3 describes our methods, Section 4 presents the results, and Sections 5 to
    27	7 discuss them.
    28	2 Previous studies
    29	Published evaluations of libraries of things are few, and most describe a single scheme in
    30	its first years. A survey of 14 schemes in England found a median of 1,150 registered
    31	borrowers per scheme after two years of operation, with wide variation by town size
    32	(Carraway Trust, 2022). The same survey reported a median household saving of GBP 60 a year
    33	among borrowers who answered its questionnaire.
    34	Repeat borrowing, the share of borrowers who borrow more than once, is often used as a sign
    35	that a scheme has become part of household routines. It was 34 percent at the Harwick Tool
    36	Library in its second year (Pemberton and Shah, 2021) and 39 percent at the Otterburn Share
    37	Shed (Lindqvist, 2023). Damage rates reported by tool libraries usually fall between 2 and 5
    38	percent of loans, with power tools at the upper end of that range (Odum, 2020).
    39	Estimates of environmental benefit vary more widely. Faraday and Mbeki (2022) estimated that
    40	a large urban scheme avoided 52 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in a year, but noted
    41	that the result depended heavily on what borrowers said they would otherwise have bought. No
    42	published study that we are aware of has followed a scheme in a town of Brackenford's size
    43	for more than one year.
    44	
    45	3 Methods
    46	3.1 The scheme
    47	At launch the catalogue held 164 items, chosen by library staff after a public consultation,
    48	and by March 2025 it had grown to 236 items. Standard members paid between GBP 1 and GBP 6
    49	per loan, depending on the item, while members receiving Council Tax Reduction borrowed free
    50	of charge. Staff checked each item on return against a written checklist and recorded any
    51	damage on the loan record.
    52	3.2 Membership and loan records
    53	We analysed the anonymised membership and loan records for the whole pilot period. Each loan
    54	record held the item, the branch, the dates of issue and return, the fee paid and any damage
    55	recorded at return. Membership records held the branch of registration and the home
    56	postcode, which we used to assign each borrower to a deprivation quintile of the Index of
    57	Multiple Deprivation.
    58	3.3 Borrower survey
    59	In February 2025 we sent an online survey to all 1,421 members who had borrowed at least one
    60	item, and paper copies were offered at all three branches. The survey asked what borrowers
    61	had used items for, what they would have done without the scheme, and how much they thought
    62	they had saved. It received 426 responses, a response rate of 30 percent.
    63	3.4 Avoided purchases and emissions
    64	We estimated avoided purchases by applying the share of survey respondents who said they
    65	would otherwise have bought each type of item to the number of different members who
    66	borrowed that type of item, so that repeat loans of the same item by the same member were
    67	counted once. Emissions were then estimated from the weight and main material of each type
    68	of item, using published factors for the manufacture of household equipment (Faraday and
    69	Mbeki, 2022).
    70	
    71	3.5 Analysis
    72	We report counts and percentages for the whole pilot and for each year, where year one runs
    73	from April 2023 to March 2024 and year two from April 2024 to March 2025. Before analysis we
    74	removed 203 loan records that staff had created to test the booking system or that had been
    75	recorded twice because of a software fault in the summer of 2023.
    76	4 Results
    77	4.1 Membership and reach
    78	By the end of March 2025, 1,936 people had registered as borrowers across the three
    79	branches. Just over half registered at Central, which is the largest branch and the only one
    80	open on Sundays (Table 1).
    81	Table 1. Registered borrowers by branch of registration, April 2023 to March 2025
    82	Branch Registered borrowers Share of registrations Concession members
    83	Central 1,012 52 percent 198
    84	Eastgate 538 28 percent 171
    85	Millbrook 386 20 percent 94
    86	All branches 1,936 100 percent 463
    87	Of the 1,490 borrowers with a usable home postcode, 611 (41 percent) lived in neighbourhoods
    88	in the two most deprived quintiles. This is close to the 40 percent of Brackenford residents
    89	who live in those neighbourhoods. The remaining 446 registrations had no usable postcode,
    90	mostly because borrowers had registered with a work address, and they are not included in
    91	this figure.
    92	
    93	4.2 Loans and repeat use
    94	Borrowers made 5,712 loans over the two years, 2,214 in year one and 3,498 in year two. This
    95	rise of 58 percent came mostly from Central and Eastgate, where reservations could be
    96	collected on the same day from the spring of 2024. Loans peaked in May and August of each
    97	year and were lowest in January.
    98	Of the 1,936 registered borrowers, 1,421 made at least one loan. Among these active
    99	borrowers, 668 borrowed more than once. That is a repeat borrowing rate of 47 percent, and
   100	it was 53 percent among those who joined in year one and 38 percent among those who joined
   101	in year two, who had less time to borrow again.
   102	The ten most borrowed items accounted for 45 percent of all loans (Table 2). Decorating and
   103	cleaning equipment was borrowed most in spring, and garden and outdoor equipment in summer.
   104	Table 2. The ten most borrowed items, April 2023 to March 2025
   105	Item Loans Share of all loans
   106	Carpet cleaner 418 7.3 percent
   107	Pressure washer 377 6.6 percent
   108	Hedge trimmer 301 5.3 percent
   109	Sewing machine 266 4.7 percent
   110	Wallpaper steamer 244 4.3 percent
   111	Gazebo 231 4.0 percent
   112	Cordless drill 219 3.8 percent
   113	Projector and screen 187 3.3 percent
   114	Four-person tent 171 3.0 percent
   115	Paint sprayer 158 2.8 percent
   116	
   117	4.3 Savings to households
   118	Survey respondents estimated that borrowing instead of buying or hiring had saved their
   119	household a median of GBP 85 over the previous twelve months. Savings were largest among
   120	those who had borrowed decorating equipment, for whom the median was GBP 120. These
   121	estimates are self-reported, and respondents may have overstated what they would otherwise
   122	have spent.
   123	Asked what they would have done without the scheme, 62 percent of respondents said they
   124	would have bought the item, 21 percent would have borrowed it from friends or family, 9
   125	percent would have hired it and 8 percent would have gone without.
   126	4.4 Avoided purchases and emissions
   127	Applying these answers to the 1,820 combinations of member and item type in the loan
   128	records, we estimate that the pilot avoided the purchase of about 1,130 items with a
   129	combined weight of 14.6 tonnes. These avoided purchases correspond to around 38 tonnes of
   130	carbon dioxide equivalent over the two years, mostly from power tools and garden machinery.
   131	The estimate is an upper bound, because it assumes that every respondent who said they would
   132	have bought an item would in fact have done so.
   133	
   134	4.5 Condition of returned items
   135	Staff recorded damage at return on 3.1 percent of loans. A further 19 items were lost or
   136	never returned, equal to 0.3 percent of loans. Repairs and replacements cost GBP 2,460 over
   137	the two years, or about 43 pence per loan. Damage was most common for power tools and garden
   138	equipment (Table 3).

   149	The pilot reached more people than most schemes of its kind, and registrations were well

results.answer:
The evaluation’s main findings were:

- The programme successfully delivered heat pumps at scale: 597 households registered interest, 318 had surveys, and 214 installations were completed between October 2022 and September 2024.
- Energy bills fell after installation. For the 162 homes with full meter data, mean annual energy spend fell from GBP 2,190 to GBP 1,818 — a 17 percent drop, or GBP 372 a year.
- Homes were warmer. In the 48 homes with temperature loggers, mean living-room temperature rose by 1.6 deg C, from 17.9 deg C to 19.5 deg C.
- Heating emissions fell substantially. Modelled emissions dropped by a mean of 2.3 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent per home per year, a 61 percent reduction, or about 490 tonnes a year across all 214 installations.
- Residents were largely positive: among survey respondents, 84 percent were satisfied or very satisfied, and 77 percent said their home was more comfortable.
- Some issues remained: 11 percent reported a fault in the first year, though most were fixed within a week.
- The main barrier to wider uptake was the cost left after the grant; the report suggests future phases may need larger grants or loans for lower-income households.

ANSWER: The evaluation found that the Kestle Bay programme achieved strong uptake and delivered lower bills, warmer homes, and major emissions reductions, with high resident satisfaction but some first-year faults and affordability remaining the main barrier to wider adoption.

     1	Warmer homes, lower bills? Evaluation of the Kestle Bay Community Heat Pump Programme, 2022 to 2024
     2	Tressider Energy Research, for Kestle Bay Community Energy. Final report, March 2025.
     3	Abstract
     4	Kestle Bay Community Energy, a community benefit society, ran a programme between October
     5	2022 and September 2024 to help owner-occupiers on the Kestle Bay peninsula replace
     6	fossil-fuel heating with air-source heat pumps. The programme combined group purchasing,
     7	free home surveys and a grant of GBP 6,000 per home. This evaluation draws on the society's
     8	records, smart meter data, temperature loggers and a follow-up survey of residents.
     9	Household energy bills fell by 21 percent on average after installation, and homes were
    10	warmer in winter. Emissions from heating fell substantially. Most residents were satisfied
    11	with their systems, although around one in ten reported a fault in the first year. The
    12	programme offers a model that other community energy groups could adapt, provided that
    13	enough installer capacity can be secured.
    14	1 Introduction
    15	Heating accounts for most household energy use and emissions in rural and coastal areas,
    16	where many homes are not connected to the gas grid and rely on heating oil or bottled gas.
    17	Air-source heat pumps can cut both bills and emissions, but take-up has been slow, held back
    18	by upfront cost, uncertainty about how well they work in older homes and a shortage of
    19	trusted installers.
    20	
    21	Kestle Bay Community Energy set out to tackle these barriers locally. It recruited
    22	households through village halls and word of mouth, arranged free home surveys, negotiated a
    23	group price with two installers and administered a grant funded by the Coastal Communities
    24	Net Zero Fund. This report evaluates the programme's uptake, its effects on energy bills,
    25	indoor temperatures and emissions, and residents' experience of their new heating systems.
    26	2 Background and previous studies
    27	Field trials of air-source heat pumps in existing homes have reported reductions in annual
    28	energy bills of between 8 and 25 percent, with the largest reductions in homes that
    29	previously used heating oil or electric storage heaters (Ashworth and Kaur, 2021). Results
    30	depend strongly on the efficiency achieved in practice, which tends to be lower in homes
    31	with small radiators or poor insulation.
    32	Community-led schemes have reported mixed uptake. In the Lowmoor scheme, 29 percent of
    33	households that registered an interest went on to have a heat pump installed (Lowmoor
    34	Energy, 2022). Studies of comfort after installation have found mean living-room
    35	temperatures rising by between 0.5 and 1.0 deg C (Brennan, 2020). Greaves and Tan (2023)
    36	estimated typical savings of 1.8 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent per home per year where
    37	a heat pump replaces a gas boiler. In a national panel of heat pump users, 79 percent said
    38	they were satisfied with their system (Heat Pump Users Panel, 2022).
    39	
    40	3 Methods
    41	3.1 The programme
    42	Households could register an interest online or at one of eleven drop-in sessions held in
    43	village halls. Each registered household was offered a free home survey by an independent
    44	assessor, who checked insulation, radiators and the electricity supply. Households that went
    45	ahead received a grant of GBP 6,000 towards the installed cost and could borrow the
    46	remainder through an interest-free loan arranged by the society. Two installers were
    47	appointed after a tender in the summer of 2022.
    48	3.2 Data sources
    49	We used four sources: the society's records of registrations, surveys and installations;
    50	half-hourly smart meter data for electricity and gas, shared with the householder's consent;
    51	installers' records of costs and faults; and a follow-up survey of residents twelve months
    52	after installation. Temperature loggers were placed in the living rooms of 48 homes that
    53	volunteered, recording every thirty minutes for one winter before and one winter after
    54	installation.
    55	3.3 Energy bills
    56	For homes with a full year of meter data before and after installation, we calculated annual
    57	spending on electricity and all heating fuels. To remove the effect of price changes, both
    58	years were valued at the unit rates and standing charges in force in October 2023. Use of
    59	heating oil and bottled gas was taken from delivery records.
    60	
    61	3.4 Emissions
    62	Emissions from heating were modelled from metered fuel and electricity use, using the
    63	government's 2023 conversion factors for each fuel. The same factor for grid electricity was
    64	used for both years, so the results do not reflect any further decarbonisation of the grid.
    65	3.5 Resident survey and temperatures
    66	The follow-up survey asked about comfort, running costs, problems and overall satisfaction,
    67	and was sent to all households with an installation. Temperatures were summarised as the
    68	mean living-room temperature between 1 December and 28 February in each winter.
    69	4 Results
    70	4.1 Uptake
    71	Between October 2022 and September 2024, 597 households registered an interest, 318 received
    72	a home survey and 214 had a heat pump installed. This conversion rate of 36 percent from
    73	registration to installation is above that reported for the Lowmoor scheme. Most households
    74	that dropped out after the survey cited the cost remaining after the grant, and a smaller
    75	number were advised that their home needed insulation work first.
    76	Table 1. Households at each stage, by main heating fuel before the programme
    77	Main heating fuel Registered interest Home survey Installed
    78	Mains gas 392 196 121
    79	Heating oil 128 79 63
    80	Electric storage heaters 51 29 21
    81	Bottled gas (LPG) 26 14 9
    82	All households 597 318 214
    83	
    84	4.2 Energy bills
    85	Complete meter data for a full year before and after installation were available for 162
    86	homes. In these homes, mean annual energy spend fell from GBP 2,190 to GBP 1,818, valued at
    87	October 2023 prices. This fall of 17 percent, or GBP 372 a year, was larger in homes that
    88	had previously used heating oil than in homes that had used mains gas.
    89	Savings also varied with the construction of the home (Table 2). For the 52 homes without
    90	complete meter data, installers' estimates suggest similar savings, but these could not be
    91	checked.
    92	Table 2. Mean annual energy spend before and after installation, by wall type, at October
    93	2023 prices
    94	Wall type Homes Before (GBP) After (GBP) Change
    95	Solid wall, built before 1919 38 2,640 2,455 -7 percent
    96	Cavity wall, insulated 81 2,050 1,600 -22 percent
    97	Cavity wall, not insulated 27 2,180 1,844 -15 percent
    98	Built after 1990 16 1,847 1,365 -26 percent
    99	All homes with full meter data 162 2,190 1,818 -17 percent
   100	
   101	4.3 Indoor temperatures
   102	In the 48 homes with temperature loggers, the mean living-room temperature from December to
   103	February rose by 1.6 deg C, from 17.9 deg C before installation to 19.5 deg C after. This
   104	gain was largest in homes that had relied on electric storage heaters, which had often been
   105	the coldest before the programme. Fewer residents reported shutting off rooms in winter to
   106	save money. The comparison is not adjusted for weather, and the second winter was on average
   107	1.1 deg C milder outdoors than the first.
   108	4.4 Emissions
   109	Modelled emissions from heating fell by a mean of 2.3 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent
   110	per home per year, a reduction of 61 percent. Across all 214 installations, this amounts to
   111	about 490 tonnes a year. These savings were roughly twice as large in oil-heated homes as in
   112	gas-heated homes, reflecting the higher carbon content of heating oil.
   113	
   114	4.5 Residents' experience
   115	Of the 214 households with an installation, 171 answered the follow-up survey, a response
   116	rate of 80 percent. Among respondents, 84 percent were satisfied or very satisfied with
   117	their heat pump, and 77 percent said their home was more comfortable than before.
   118	Twenty-three households, 11 percent of those with an installation, reported a fault in the
   119	first year (Table 3). Most faults were fixed within a week, but three households were
   120	without heating for more than five days.
   121	Table 3. Faults reported in the first year after installation, by type
   122	Type of fault Households Median days to fix
   123	Controls or thermostat 9 2
   124	Hot water cylinder 6 4
   125	Outdoor unit 4 6
   126	Electrical supply 2 3
   127	Refrigerant leak 2 9
   128	All faults 23 3
   129	5 Discussion
   130	The programme turned a larger share of interested households into installations than
   131	comparable community schemes, which suggests that free surveys and a trusted local
   132	organisation can overcome some of the barriers to take-up. The cost remaining after the
   133	grant was the main reason for dropping out, and future phases may need larger grants or
   134	loans for households on low incomes.
   135	The fall in bills is within the range reported in field trials, and the larger savings in
   136	oil-heated homes match earlier findings. Savings in older solid-wall homes were smaller,
   137	which supports the case for combining heat pumps with insulation where that is affordable.
   138	
   139	6 Limitations
   140	There was no comparison group of homes that kept their old heating, so changes in bills and
   141	temperatures may partly reflect other changes in households. Meter data were complete for
   142	only 162 of the 214 homes, and temperature loggers were placed in only 48 volunteer homes,
   143	which may not be typical. Emissions were modelled rather than measured. The follow-up survey
   144	was carried out by the society itself, which may have encouraged favourable answers.
   145	7 Conclusions

   147	in an area with many older and off-grid homes. Households saved money and were warmer, and

     2	
     3	From the Head of Libraries, Brackenford Council. For the committee meeting on 18 November 2025.
     4	
     5	Purpose
     6	
     7	This briefing summarises the independent evaluation of the Library of Things pilot by Northfold Social Research and sets out the library service's proposals for the scheme's future.
     8	
     9	What the evaluation found
    10	
    11	The pilot exceeded its target of 1,500 registered borrowers, and use grew in the second year. Borrowers reported that they saved money, and most items came back in good condition. The service accepts the evaluation's findings, with one exception set out below.
    12

    14	
    15	Our own repair log records damage on 6.8 percent of loans, more than twice the evaluation's figure. The difference arises because the evaluation counted only damage noted by staff when an item was returned, while the repair log also includes faults found at the next safety check or by the next borrower. We consider the repair log the better measure of the cost of wear and tear.
    16	
    17	Proposals
    18	
    19	We propose to continue the scheme for a further three years and to open a fourth collection point at Northfield library from April 2026, at an estimated additional cost of GBP 31,000 a year. Members receiving Council Tax Reduction would continue to borrow free of charge.

    22	
    23	The committee is asked to approve the continuation and extension of the Library of Things as set out above, funded from the libraries budget and from loan fees.

- The first phase had closed in September with **214 installations**.
- Waiting times had improved, with a **median of 9 weeks** between survey and installation, down from **14 weeks** in the first year.

- To set a target of **150 further installations by March 2026**.

ANSWER: The board noted strong first-phase delivery and shorter waiting times, but also an installer shortage after Brightwater Heating withdrew. [1.1] s1:
  p.1: Borrowing instead of buying: evaluation of the Brackenford Library of Things pilot, April 2023 to March 2025
  p.1 §Abstract: The Brackenford Library of Things lends household tools and equipment from three branch libraries for a small fee. This report evaluates the first two years of the pilot, from April 2023 to March 2025, using membership and loan records, a survey of borrowers and the checks that staff make when items are returned.
  p.1: Borrowers reported modest savings, and most items came back in good condition.
  p.1 §1 Introduction: Libraries of things apply the familiar library model to objects that households need only occasionally, such as drills, gazebos and sewing machines. Their supporters argue that borrowing saves money, reduces the number of rarely used items that people buy, and brings people into libraries who would not otherwise visit.
  p.2: Items could be reserved online and collected from any of the three branches, and loans lasted up to seven days. This report sets out what the pilot achieved against the aims agreed with the funder: to reach a broad range of residents, to build regular use, to save households money and to reduce waste.
  p.3 §3.3 Borrower survey: The survey asked what borrowers had used items for, what they would have done without the scheme, and how much they thought they had saved.
  p.3 §3.4 Avoided purchases and emissions: Emissions were then estimated from the weight and main material of each type of item, using published factors for the manufacture of household equipment (Faraday and Mbeki, 2022).
  p.4 §4.1 Membership and reach: By the end of March 2025, 1,936 people had registered as borrowers across the three branches.
  p.6 §4.3 Savings to households: Survey respondents estimated that borrowing instead of buying or hiring had saved their household a median of GBP 85 over the previous twelve months. Savings were largest among those who had borrowed decorating equipment, for whom the median was GBP 120.
  p.7 §5 Discussion: The pilot reached more people than most schemes of its kind, and registrations were well above the median reported for English schemes after two years.
  p.7: The scheme's main value to many members may lie less in money saved than in access to equipment they could not store or could not justify buying.
  p.8 §7 Conclusions: The Library of Things pilot met its aims for reach and regular use, and it delivered savings and environmental benefits that, while uncertain in size, point in the right direction.

  p.1: Warmer homes, lower bills?
  p.1 §Abstract: Household energy bills fell by 21 percent on average after installation, and homes were warmer in winter. Emissions from heating fell substantially. Most residents were satisfied with their systems, although around one in ten reported a fault in the first year.
  p.3 §3.2 Data sources: Temperature loggers were placed in the living rooms of 48 homes that volunteered, recording every thirty minutes for one winter before and one winter after installation.
  p.4 §3.5 Resident survey and temperatures: The follow-up survey asked about comfort, running costs, problems and overall satisfaction, and was sent to all households with an installation.
  p.4 §4.1 Uptake: Between October 2022 and September 2024, 597 households registered an interest, 318 received a home survey and 214 had a heat pump installed. This conversion rate of 36 percent from registration to installation is above that reported for the Lowmoor scheme.
  p.5 §4.2 Energy bills: Complete meter data for a full year before and after installation were available for 162 homes.
  p.5: For the 52 homes without complete meter data, installers' estimates suggest similar savings, but these could not be checked.
  p.6 §4.3 Indoor temperatures: In the 48 homes with temperature loggers, the mean living-room temperature from December to February rose by 1.6 deg C, from 17.9 deg C before installation to 19.5 deg C after. This gain was largest in homes that had relied on electric storage heaters, which had often been the coldest before the programme. Fewer residents reported shutting off rooms in winter to save money.
  p.7 §4.5 Residents' experience: Twenty-three households, 11 percent of those with an installation, reported a fault in the first year (Table 3). Most faults were fixed within a week, but three households were without heating for more than five days.
  p.7: Faults reported in the first year after installation, by type Type of fault Households Median days to fix
  p.7: Table 3. Faults reported in the first year after installation, by type [Type of fault Households Median days to fix]
    Controls or thermostat 9 2
  p.7 §5 Discussion: The programme turned a larger share of interested households into installations than comparable community schemes, which suggests that free surveys and a trusted local organisation can overcome some of the barriers to take-up.
  p.7: The fall in bills is within the range reported in field trials, and the larger savings in oil-heated homes match earlier findings. Savings in older solid-wall homes were smaller, which supports the case for combining heat pumps with insulation where that is affordable.
  p.8 §6 Limitations: There was no comparison group of homes that kept their old heating, so changes in bills and temperatures may partly reflect other changes in households. Meter data were complete for only 162 of the 214 homes, and temperature loggers were placed in only 48 volunteer homes, which may not be typical.
  p.8 §7 Conclusions: The Kestle Bay programme shows that a community energy group can deliver heat pumps at scale in an area with many older and off-grid homes. Households saved money and were warmer, and emissions from heating fell sharply. We recommend that the next phase gives priority to oil-heated homes, offers insulation alongside heat pumps in solid-wall homes, and secures more installer capacity.

Reviews/Heat pump programme board notes.md
     1	Warmer homes, lower bills? Evaluation of the Kestle Bay Community Heat Pump Programme, 2022 to 2024
     2	Tressider Energy Research, for Kestle Bay Community Energy. Final report, March 2025.
     3	Abstract
     4	Kestle Bay Community Energy, a community benefit society, ran a programme between October
     5	2022 and September 2024 to help owner-occupiers on the Kestle Bay peninsula replace
     6	fossil-fuel heating with air-source heat pumps. The programme combined group purchasing,
     7	free home surveys and a grant of GBP 6,000 per home. This evaluation draws on the society's
     8	records, smart meter data, temperature loggers and a follow-up survey of residents.
     9	Household energy bills fell by 21 percent on average after installation, and homes were
    10	warmer in winter. Emissions from heating fell substantially. Most residents were satisfied
    11	with their systems, although around one in ten reported a fault in the first year. The
    12	programme offers a model that other community energy groups could adapt, provided that
    13	enough installer capacity can be secured.
    14	1 Introduction
    15	Heating accounts for most household energy use and emissions in rural and coastal areas,
    16	where many homes are not connected to the gas grid and rely on heating oil or bottled gas.
    17	Air-source heat pumps can cut both bills and emissions, but take-up has been slow, held back
    18	by upfront cost, uncertainty about how well they work in older homes and a shortage of
    19	trusted installers.
    20	
    21	Kestle Bay Community Energy set out to tackle these barriers locally. It recruited
    22	households through village halls and word of mouth, arranged free home surveys, negotiated a
    23	group price with two installers and administered a grant funded by the Coastal Communities
    24	Net Zero Fund. This report evaluates the programme's uptake, its effects on energy bills,
    25	indoor temperatures and emissions, and residents' experience of their new heating systems.
    26	2 Background and previous studies
    27	Field trials of air-source heat pumps in existing homes have reported reductions in annual
    28	energy bills of between 8 and 25 percent, with the largest reductions in homes that
    29	previously used heating oil or electric storage heaters (Ashworth and Kaur, 2021). Results
    30	depend strongly on the efficiency achieved in practice, which tends to be lower in homes
    31	with small radiators or poor insulation.
    32	Community-led schemes have reported mixed uptake. In the Lowmoor scheme, 29 percent of
    33	households that registered an interest went on to have a heat pump installed (Lowmoor
    34	Energy, 2022). Studies of comfort after installation have found mean living-room
    35	temperatures rising by between 0.5 and 1.0 deg C (Brennan, 2020). Greaves and Tan (2023)
    36	estimated typical savings of 1.8 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent per home per year where
    37	a heat pump replaces a gas boiler. In a national panel of heat pump users, 79 percent said
    38	they were satisfied with their system (Heat Pump Users Panel, 2022).
    39	
    40	3 Methods
    41	3.1 The programme
    42	Households could register an interest online or at one of eleven drop-in sessions held in
    43	village halls. Each registered household was offered a free home survey by an independent
    44	assessor, who checked insulation, radiators and the electricity supply. Households that went
    45	ahead received a grant of GBP 6,000 towards the installed cost and could borrow the
    46	remainder through an interest-free loan arranged by the society. Two installers were
    47	appointed after a tender in the summer of 2022.
    48	3.2 Data sources
    49	We used four sources: the society's records of registrations, surveys and installations;
    50	half-hourly smart meter data for electricity and gas, shared with the householder's consent;
    51	installers' records of costs and faults; and a follow-up survey of residents twelve months
    52	after installation. Temperature loggers were placed in the living rooms of 48 homes that
    53	volunteered, recording every thirty minutes for one winter before and one winter after
    54	installation.
    55	3.3 Energy bills
    56	For homes with a full year of meter data before and after installation, we calculated annual
    57	spending on electricity and all heating fuels. To remove the effect of price changes, both
    58	years were valued at the unit rates and standing charges in force in October 2023. Use of
    59	heating oil and bottled gas was taken from delivery records.

    61	3.4 Emissions
    62	Emissions from heating were modelled from metered fuel and electricity use, using the
    63	government's 2023 conversion factors for each fuel. The same factor for grid electricity was
    64	used for both years, so the results do not reflect any further decarbonisation of the grid.
    65	3.5 Resident survey and temperatures
    66	The follow-up survey asked about comfort, running costs, problems and overall satisfaction,
    67	and was sent to all households with an installation. Temperatures were summarised as the
    68	mean living-room temperature between 1 December and 28 February in each winter.
    69	4 Results
    70	4.1 Uptake
    71	Between October 2022 and September 2024, 597 households registered an interest, 318 received
    72	a home survey and 214 had a heat pump installed. This conversion rate of 36 percent from
    73	registration to installation is above that reported for the Lowmoor scheme. Most households
    74	that dropped out after the survey cited the cost remaining after the grant, and a smaller
    75	number were advised that their home needed insulation work first.

    79	Heating oil 128 79 63
    80	Electric storage heaters 51 29 21
    81	Bottled gas (LPG) 26 14 9
    82	All households 597 318 214
    83	
    84	4.2 Energy bills
    85	Complete meter data for a full year before and after installation were available for 162
    86	homes. In these homes, mean annual energy spend fell from GBP 2,190 to GBP 1,818, valued at
    87	October 2023 prices. This fall of 17 percent, or GBP 372 a year, was larger in homes that
    88	had previously used heating oil than in homes that had used mains gas.
    89	Savings also varied with the construction of the home (Table 2). For the 52 homes without
    90	complete meter data, installers' estimates suggest similar savings, but these could not be
    91	checked.

    93	2023 prices
